pl-l3d22c1-d1e115.summary: Raises the question whether Christ was a man during the three days of death.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e118.summary: Gives an objection: some think not, because he was dead, and a dead man is not a man.
claims: Some deny that Christ was a man in death.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e121.summary: Adds a second objection: if he was a man then, he was mortal or immortal; but not mortal, since dead, and not immortal, since that came only after the resurrection.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e125.summary: Replies that although the man was dead, the God-man was in death truly man, neither mortal nor immortal. Such subtleties apply to creatures, but the sacrament of faith is free from philosophical arguments.
claims: Christ in death was truly man, neither mortal nor immortal.
The mystery of faith is not bound by dialectical arguments.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e128.summary: Quotes Ambrose: take away arguments where faith is sought; let dialectic be silent; fishermen are believed, not dialecticians.
claims: Faith rests on the apostles, not on dialectic.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e137.summary: States the position: in Christ's death God was truly man and yet dead, and man neither mortal nor immortal, because united to soul and flesh separated from each other. God is called man, and man God, in a different sense from Martin or John: because of the assumption of a man, that is, of soul and flesh.
claims: In death God was truly man, united to separated soul and flesh.
'God is man' is said by reason of the assumption of soul and flesh.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e140.summary: Quotes Augustine: such was that assumption that made God man and man God.
claims: The assumption makes God man and man God.

pl-l3d22c1-d1e149.summary: Concludes: since the assumption did not fail through death, God remained truly united to the man, and so God was man, being united to soul and flesh; and the man was dead because soul was divided from flesh. He was dead by their mutual separation, man by the union of each with himself. He was not then man as subsisting from soul and flesh joined together, the sense in which another is called man, though perhaps he was man in this way before death and after the resurrection.
claims: The assumption did not fail through death.
In death Christ was man by the union of soul and flesh with himself, not by their union with each other.
He was dead because soul and flesh were separated.

pl-l3d22c1.summary: Asks whether Christ was a man during the three days of death. Some deny it, since a dead man is not a man, and a man must be mortal or immortal. Lombard replies that the dead God-man was truly man though neither mortal nor immortal; such subtleties hold among creatures, but the sacrament of faith is free from philosophical arguments, as Ambrose says. God is called man, and man God, not as Martin or John is a man, but by assumption of soul and flesh; since this assumption did not fail in death, God was man by union with both, and dead by their separation from each other, though not man as subsisting from soul and flesh joined.
claims: Christ was truly man during the three days of death.
During death Christ was neither mortal nor immortal.
God is man by assumption of soul and flesh, not as an individual man is a man.
Christ was man by union with soul and flesh, and dead by their separation from each other.
The sacrament of faith is free from philosophical arguments.
